obtained.how: the publisher's typeset PDF posted on the first author's lab website (Vander Zanden lab, Center for Limnology, University of Wisconsin–Madison), 13 pages; Fig. 3 read on the page image

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the first page (PDF p. 1)
bibliography.note: authors, year, title, Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences 68(1): 170–182, doi:10.1139/F10-157 all match (a Perspective based on the 2009 J.C. Stevenson Memorial Lecture). printed page = PDF page + 169

claims.claim: airborne terrestrial particulate carbon averaged 1.88 g C per meter of shoreline per year across seven estimates, declining exponentially away from the shore
claims.source_value: 1.88 g C m⁻¹ yr⁻¹ is the parameter (s) of a negative exponential DISTRIBUTION fitted to the frequency histogram of seven per-shoreline deposition estimates (Fig. 3d, values about 0.5–5.5), from which deposition values were drawn for 5,000 simulated lakes; the exponential describes the spread among lakes, not a decline with distance from shore
claims.location: p. 177 (PDF p. 8), Modeling land-to-lake flux; p. 176 (PDF p. 7), Fig. 3d
claims.quote: we fit a negative exponential model to the Dshore estimates
claims.conditions: the seven estimates (from Preston et al. 2008) were "collected using diverse sampling methods (mesh size, seasonality, and sampling intensity)"
claims.note: what the source says about distance from shore is separate: leaf litter falls mostly within 10 m of shore, and fine POC is elevated near shore "though there is notable deposition extending substantial distances out into the lake" (p. 172). Say "seven estimates, fitted with a negative exponential distribution of mean ~1.9 g C per m of shore per year"

claims.claim: terrestrial insects are "rarely dominant in lentic fish diets"
claims.quote: terrestrial insects are rarely dominant in lentic fish diets, they are commonly present
claims.conditions: review statement (Hunt 1975; Weidel et al. 2008); the same paragraph gives exceptions (bleak ~84 % terrestrial insects, Mehner et al. 2005; Castle Lake trout > 30 %)

claims.claim: lakes receive leaves mainly within about 10 m of a forested shore
claims.quote: with most leaf litter inputs to lakes occurring within 10 m of shore
claims.conditions: the source cites Gasith & Hasler 1976 and France & Peters 1995; a rapid decline with distance from shore
claims.note: "forested" is the paper's word, not the source's

claims.claim: across 49 whole-lake estimates, median benthic secondary production was 2.3 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹, insects made up about 70 % of it, and 30 ± 4 % of insect production emerged
claims.source_value: only the production figure rests on 49 whole-lake estimates (median 2.3 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹, right-skewed); the insect share is 0.70 ± 0.33 from 28 estimates and the emerging fraction 0.30 ± 0.04 from 18 (both given as mean ± 1 SD)
claims.location: p. 176 (PDF p. 7), Results: lake-to-land and Fig. 3a–c
claims.quote: approximately 30% of insect production leaves lakes in the form of insect emergence
claims.conditions: literature compilation, most production estimates from the 1960s–70s International Biological Programme (only 14 of 49 after 1980); n = 49, 28 and 18 (p. 176)
claims.note: the ± 0.04 is labelled an SD, but Fig. 3c's 18 values run from about 0.1 to 0.7 (my reading of the histogram: SD ≈ 0.19, so ± 0.04 matches a standard error). Say "about 30 % (18 estimates, ~10–70 %)"

claims.claim: across 49 whole-lake estimates, 0.30 ± 0.04 of insect production emerged
claims.source_value: the emerging fraction comes from 18 estimates, not 49 (0.30 ± 0.04, labelled mean ± 1 SD; the values span about 0.1–0.7 in Fig. 3c)

claims.claim: applied to Upper, these figures give an emergence export of roughly 7–11 mg P and 70–110 mg N m⁻² yr⁻¹ (project estimate)
claims.quote: Nitrogen and phosphorus content in insects is high, roughly 10% and 1%
claims.conditions: inputs from this source: median production 2.3 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹ × insect share 0.70 × emerging fraction 0.30 = 0.48 g C m⁻² yr⁻¹; insects ~10 % N and ~1 % P (also given by Dreyer et al. 2015)
claims.note: working: 0.48 g C at ~45 % C (the note's C:dry ratio, not from this source) ≈ 1.07 g dry → ~11 mg P and ~107 mg N; the note's lower end (0.3 g C → 0.7 g dry → 7 mg P) is a rounding down, not derived. It mixes a median with means, and the emerging fraction alone spans ~0.1–0.7, so the true uncertainty is several-fold wider than 7–11

claims.quote: approximately 30% of insect production leaves lakes in the form of insect emergence
claims.conditions: mean of 18 literature estimates, spread about 0.1–0.7 (Fig. 3c); independent of lake area

tried.note: publisher refuses scripts (OpenAlex lists it as bronze open access)

notes: Other values: with typical emergence and deposition, airborne terrestrial carbon into a lake exceeds the insect carbon leaving it in lakes smaller than about 2,000 ha (p. 178), so for both Hot Brook lakes the land-to-lake airborne CARBON flux should exceed emergence, while in nutrient terms the insects weigh more (insects ~10 % N, 1 % P against nutrient-poor plant litter, p. 179); fine POC deposition can extend far into a lake (Preston et al. 2008); in Wisconsin, shoreline deposition rose with lake area across 16 lakes of 0.1–184 ha (Preston 2009, p. 179); insect deposition on land declines as a negative exponential with distance from shore (Gratton & Vander Zanden 2009, p. 173). show.mjs also lists these citing sentences under VanderZanden_etal_2011 (a different 2011 paper); they belong here.
